item.title: South Korea May exports drop 1.3% year on year; estimated -2.4%
item.description:
South Korea May exports drop 1.3% year on year; estimated -2.4%

SEOUL (Reuters) — South Korea’s exports are expected to have fallen 1.3% year on year in May, according to a Reuters poll, marking the first decline since January. This comes as the impact of U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs offsets strong demand for semiconductors [1].

Exports out of Asia’s fourth-largest economy are forecast to have fallen 2.7% this month from a year earlier, according to a median of 16 economists. This decline is primarily attributed to a 14.6% drop in shipments to the U.S. and a 7.2% decline in shipments to China [1].

In April, exports unexpectedly rose 3.7%, with robust chip sales, particularly high-end AI products, offsetting declines in car exports hit by Trump’s tariffs [1]. However, in the first 20 days of May, exports fell 2.4%, with U.S. and Chinese shipments dropping significantly [1].

Trump has imposed 25% duties on automobiles and steel products and suggested more tariffs on semiconductors and pharmaceuticals. His reciprocal tariffs, currently on pause for negotiations, are expected to resume by July 9 and August 12 [1].

South Korea’s imports are projected to have fallen 3.1% in May, following a 2.7% drop in April, according to the survey conducted on May 19-28. The median estimate for the country’s trade balance stood at a surplus of $4.61 billion, compared to $4.88 billion in the previous month [1].

South Korea's record-high trade surpluses with the U.S. are expected to narrow as companies continue to invest in the U.S. market, according to the Korea International Trade Association (KITA) [2]. In 2024, 46.8% of U.S. imports from South Korea were intermediate goods shipped to the country for direct investments [2].

The U.S. has demanded that South Korea resolve the large trade imbalance between the countries during recent trade talks. South Korea earned a $55.6 billion surplus from trade with the U.S. in 2024, up 25% from 2023 [3]. The two countries have agreed to address the trade imbalance and are discussing non-tariff measures, economic security, and digital trade [3].

The trade talks will continue under the next government, as South Korea is holding a snap presidential election on June 3.

item.description:
South Korea trade balance (May): Actual KRW 6.94B, expected KRW 4.61B, previous KRW 4.88B

South Korea's trade balance for May showed a significant change from expectations, with actual exports and imports revealing a more complex picture than anticipated. The country's exports are expected to have fallen for the first time in four months, according to a Reuters poll [1]. This decline is attributed to the impact of U.S. President Donald Trump's tariffs offsetting robust demand for semiconductors.

The Reuters poll predicted a 2.7% year-on-year decline in exports in May, which would be the first such decline since January. This prediction was based on a median of 16 economists' forecasts [1]. The actual data released on June 1, 2025, indicated a trade balance of KRW 6.94 billion, which was higher than the expected KRW 4.61 billion but lower than the previous month's KRW 4.88 billion.

The first 20 days of May saw exports fall by 2.4%, with shipments to the U.S. dropping 14.6% and those to China declining 7.2% [1]. The robust sales of high-end semiconductors for artificial intelligence did not fully offset the decline in car exports hit by U.S. tariffs [1]. The uncertainty around the U.S. tariffs and the ongoing trade war between the U.S. and China has contributed to the slowdown in global trade, as observed by economists [1].

South Korea's imports are projected to have fallen by 3.1% in May, following a 2.7% drop in April [1]. The trade balance for May stood at a surplus of KRW 4.61 billion, compared to KRW 4.88 billion in the previous month [1].

The Bank of Korea (BOK) has responded to these economic challenges by cutting interest rates to support the economy. The BOK lowered its benchmark interest rate to 2.50% on May 29, 2025, just days before South Korea's presidential election [3]. This move is part of the central bank's efforts to mitigate the impact of U.S. tariffs and stimulate economic growth.

The trade data and the BOK's monetary policy indicate that South Korea is navigating through challenging economic conditions. The country's exports are expected to fall in the second quarter, and the trade balance has shown mixed results compared to expectations [1]. As South Korea prepares for a new presidential leadership, the economic recovery will be a key focus for the incoming administration.

item.description:
South Korea imports (YoY) (May): Actual -5.3%, expected -3.1%, previous -2.7%

Seoul, June 1, 2025 - South Korea's central bank, the Bank of Korea (BOK), delivered a dovish interest rate cut on May 29, reducing the benchmark rate to 2.50%. This move came amidst ongoing economic challenges, particularly the impact of U.S. tariffs, and ahead of the country's presidential election scheduled for June 3. The BOK's decision was widely anticipated and aligns with a broader global trend of monetary easing.

The BOK's rate cut, the fourth in its current easing cycle, was accompanied by a downward revision of its economic outlook for the year to 0.8%. Four of the BOK's seven board members indicated that the door remains open for further rate cuts in the near term. This dovish stance reflects the central bank's intention to support economic recovery and mitigate the effects of U.S. trade policies.

The decision was welcomed by presidential candidates from both major political parties, who have pledged immediate fiscal stimulus packages to counter the economic slowdown. The BOK's governor, Rhee Chang-yong, acknowledged potential downside risks from U.S. tariffs but remained optimistic about the possibility of trade improvement following a U.S. court's recent decision to block certain tariffs.

Analysts predict that South Korea's monetary policy will be more accommodative by the end of this year compared to those of the U.S. and Australia, and broadly on par with Canada's and New Zealand's. The consensus among analysts is that the BOK may cut rates by an additional two times, bringing the policy rate down to 2.00% by the end of the year.

South Korea's economic performance has been affected by the uncertainty caused by the U.S. tariffs, with the country's economy unexpectedly shrinking in the first quarter. The latest data shows that South Korea's imports (YoY) in May were down by 5.3%, falling short of the expected decrease of 3.1% and a previous drop of 2.7%. This significant decline in imports underscores the economic challenges posed by the global trade environment.

The BOK's latest move underscores its commitment to supporting the South Korean economy through monetary policy, aiming to foster growth amidst the ongoing geopolitical uncertainties. As the presidential election approaches, the focus will shift to how the new administration will address economic challenges and implement fiscal stimulus measures.

item.title: BoE Breeden: Labor market loosening times
item.description:
BoE Breeden: Labor market loosening times

The U.S. labor market has shown signs of easing, as evidenced by a recent rise in unemployment claims. According to the latest report from the Labor Department, initial claims for state unemployment benefits increased by 14,000 to a seasonally adjusted 240,000 for the week ended May 24 [1]. This figure exceeded the economists' forecast of 230,000, signaling a potential weakening of labor market conditions.

The Federal Reserve, in its May policy meeting minutes, acknowledged the risk of a weakening job market [1]. The minutes highlighted that while labor market conditions were broadly in balance, there was a risk of weakening in coming months, largely due to uncertainties surrounding trade policies and other government policies [1].

Economic uncertainty, fueled by President Trump's aggressive trade policies, has contributed to increased layoffs and employer hesitancy in hiring [1]. The U.S. trade court's ruling blocking most of Trump's tariffs from going into effect has provided some relief, but it has also added another layer of uncertainty over the economy [1].

The Bank of America Institute reported a sharp rise in higher-income households receiving unemployment benefits between February and April compared to the same period last year [1]. This indicates a broader impact on the labor market, with both higher- and lower-income households experiencing job losses.

The Federal Reserve has kept its benchmark overnight interest rate in the 4.25%-4.50% range since December, as officials struggle to estimate the impact of Trump's tariffs on inflation and economic growth [1]. The elevated continuing claims, which reflect companies' hesitancy to increase headcount due to economic uncertainty, also suggest that the labor market may be experiencing a slowdown [1].

In addition to trade policies, federal employment cuts could also impact the labor market. Policies from the Trump administration, which aim for a broad reduction in federal government workers and spending, could push unemployment higher [2]. While the near-term impact is muted, the aggregate effect of these job losses could begin to weigh on headline numbers by late 2025 [2].

The UK's Autumn Budget has also introduced significant inflationary risks, which could impact global financial markets [3]. The budget's planned GBP100 billion in public investment over five years and increased borrowing requirements could drive up gilt yields, potentially affecting interest rates and economic growth [3].

In conclusion, the U.S. labor market is showing signs of easing, driven by economic uncertainty and trade policies. The Federal Reserve and other economic indicators suggest that the labor market may continue to weaken in the coming months. Investors and financial professionals should closely monitor these developments and their potential impact on the broader economy.

item.title: Turkey's president: Turkey working to organize Russia-Ukraine meeting in Istanbul
item.description:
Turkey's president: Turkey working to organize Russia-Ukraine meeting in Istanbul

Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has expressed optimism about the possibility of organizing a second round of peace talks between Russia and Ukraine in Istanbul. Speaking to reporters on a flight from Azerbaijan, Erdogan stated that the recent momentum in peace efforts, driven by Russia's proposal to hold talks in Istanbul on June 2, is an opportunity to reach lasting peace [3].

The proposed meeting is part of ongoing efforts to resolve the ongoing conflict between Russia and Ukraine. The talks are scheduled to take place on June 2 and are expected to include representatives from both countries, as well as the national security advisors of the UK, Germany, and France [1]. However, Ukraine has not yet confirmed its attendance at the talks.

The meeting comes amid increasing international pressure on Russia to agree to a ceasefire. In a recent UN security council meeting, the US proposed a 30-day land, air, sea, and critical infrastructure ceasefire, warning that further sanctions could be imposed if Russia does not accept the proposal [2].

Erdogan's comments reflect Turkey's ongoing diplomatic efforts to facilitate peace between the two warring nations. Turkey has maintained good relations with both sides since the start of the conflict and has hosted previous rounds of peace talks. The latest proposal for talks in Istanbul follows a meeting between Russian and Ukrainian delegates in May, where they agreed to trade 1,000 prisoners of war and share their views on the contours of a truce [3].

The potential success of the Istanbul talks remains uncertain, but Erdogan's optimism highlights the ongoing diplomatic efforts to bring an end to the conflict. As the talks approach, the international community will be closely monitoring the situation, hoping for a resolution that brings peace to the region.

item.title: A bridge collapse causes a train to derail in Russia, killing at least 3 people, officials say
item.description:
A bridge collapse causes a train to derail in Russia, killing at least 3 people, officials say

MOSCOW — A passenger train derailed in western Russia late Saturday after a bridge collapsed due to what local officials described as "illegal interference." At least three people were killed, and 28 others were injured [1].

The incident occurred in the Bryansk region, en route from Moscow to Klimov. The bridge, which was damaged as a result of illegal interference in transport operations, caused the train to come off its tracks [1].

Emergency services and government officials are working at the scene to provide assistance to the victims. The regional governor, Alexander Bogomaz, stated that everything is being done to help those affected [1].

This is not the first time alleged saboteurs have used explosive devices to derail a train in Russia. In November 2023, a terrorism investigation was launched after explosions derailed 19 cars in the Ryzan Region [2].

The exact cause of the bridge collapse and the number of casualties are still under investigation. Moscow Railways has stated that other train traffic is not impacted by the incident [2].

item.title: Norway set to reject calls for blanket ban by wealth fund on companies in Israeli-occupied areas, source says - Reuters
item.description:
Norway set to reject calls for blanket ban by wealth fund on companies in Israeli-occupied areas, source says - Reuters

Norway's parliament is poised to reject campaigners' calls for its $1.8 trillion wealth fund to impose a blanket ban on companies selling products and services in Israeli-occupied areas. According to a person familiar with the process, a majority in the Norwegian parliament's finance committee has decided that only companies directly linked to violations of international law should be excluded from the fund's portfolio [1].

The International Court of Justice ruled last year that Israel's occupation of Palestinian territories is illegal and should be ended as soon as possible. This ruling has fueled campaigner demands for Norway to mirror its 2022 action against Russia, when the fund was instructed to divest all Russian holdings days after the invasion of Ukraine [2].

However, the parliamentary finance committee's stance signals a rejection of a blanket ban on Israeli companies or multinational corporations whose products and services are available in the occupied Palestinian territories. The committee decided that only companies selling specific products for Israeli settlers, such as surveillance equipment, should be excluded from the fund's portfolio [1].

The committee's decision is part of its assessment of the government's annual filing on the wealth fund, which is due to be debated in parliament on June 4, with a vote expected the same day. Lawmakers are expected to vote along their parties' lines as set in the parliamentary finance committee's conclusions [1].

The decision will be closely watched, given Norway's fund, which owns 1.5% of the world's listed shares across 9,000 companies, is seen as a leader in the field of investing focused on environmental, social, and governance issues [1].

item.title: SEC casts doubt on RexOsprey bid to launch staking ETH, Solana ETFs
item.description:
SEC casts doubt on RexOsprey bid to launch staking ETH, Solana ETFs

The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has expressed concerns regarding RexOsprey's attempt to launch staking ETFs for Ethereum (ETH) and Solana (SOL), potentially blocking their listing in the stock market. This development comes as the SEC has been increasingly cautious about the legal classification of staking activities and ETFs in the cryptocurrency space.

RexOsprey, a firm known for its innovative approaches to cryptocurrency investment products, filed a prospectus with the SEC to launch two groundbreaking ETFs focused on staking ETH and SOL. Instead of opting for the traditional 19b-4 process, RexOsprey chose the 40-Act filing under the Investment Company Act of 1940, a move that aims to expedite the launch of these ETFs [1].

However, the SEC has raised concerns that the proposed ETFs may not legally qualify as investment companies under federal securities law. In a letter sent to ETF Opportunities Trust, the SEC expressed doubts about the funds' compliance with the legal definition of an investment company, a designation required for listing in the stock market [2].

The SEC's concerns stem from the staking activities involved in the ETFs, which allow investors to earn rewards by pledging tokens to help operate the blockchain. The agency has previously stated that such activities may not be considered securities, but the recent regulatory environment has led to confusion and uncertainty [3].

Despite the SEC's concerns, RexOsprey remains optimistic about the future of these ETFs. Greg Collett, general counsel at Rex Financial, stated that the company believes it can address the SEC's concerns and does not intend to launch the funds until compliance is ensured. The SEC, however, has not yet provided a definitive timeline for resolving these issues [2].

The delay in the approval of these ETFs is not the only challenge facing the cryptocurrency ETF market in the United States. The SEC has also delayed decisions on Grayscale's Avalanche and Cardano spot ETF applications, affecting the launch of these products [1].

In conclusion, the SEC's concerns regarding RexOsprey's staking ETFs highlight the ongoing regulatory uncertainty in the cryptocurrency ETF market. While the SEC has provided some clarity on staking activities, the legal classification of these ETFs remains a contentious issue. Investors and financial professionals should closely monitor the SEC's ongoing review process to stay informed about potential developments in this rapidly evolving market.

item.title: Britain to allocate 1.5 billion pounds for bomb factories
item.description:
Britain to allocate 1.5 billion pounds for bomb factories

The British government has announced plans to allocate £1.5 billion for the construction of at least six new munitions factories as part of its Strategic Defence Review. The investment, part of a 10-year plan for military equipment and services, aims to bolster the country's industrial base and enhance its defence capabilities [2].

Defence Secretary John Healey stated that the new factories will be responsible for producing up to 7,000 long-range weapons, including attack drones and precision missiles. The first factory is expected to be operational within the next few years, with all six sites ready by the end of the current Parliament [1][2].

The announcement comes amidst ongoing criticism from opposition parties and defence analysts who argue that the government's plans are not sufficient or timely. Shadow Defence Secretary James Cartlidge described the review as a "damp squib," asserting that Labour has wasted time and that the Treasury has prioritized penny-pinching over rapid rearmament [1].

Despite the criticism, the government maintains that the new weapons will serve as a deterrent against potential adversaries, particularly Russia. The arsenal is expected to include advanced long-range missiles such as Storm Shadows and hypersonic missiles, as well as kamikaze drones like the HX-2 [1].

The investment in munitions factories is part of a broader effort to improve the UK's defence infrastructure. The Ministry of Defence also announced plans to spend an additional £1.5 billion to address the poor housing conditions for the country's armed forces [2].

The Strategic Defence Review, expected to be published on Monday, is a significant step in Britain's efforts to strengthen its military capabilities and secure its position in the global arena. The investment in munitions factories is likely to have a positive impact on the country's economy, creating around 1,800 new jobs [2].

item.description:
Britain to commit to purchasing 7,000 long-range weapons: Telegraph

In a significant move to bolster its military capabilities, Britain has announced plans to purchase 7,000 long-range weapons. The decision was made in response to warnings from military leaders that the UK's current fighting force is no longer effective [1]. The announcement comes as part of a broader Strategic Defence Review, which will outline the future of the Army, Navy, and Air Force.

Defence Secretary John Healey will unveil the details of this initiative on Monday, including a £1.5 billion investment in new bomb factories. These factories will have the capacity to massively ramp up production of artillery shells and explosives, ensuring that Britain is always ready for potential conflicts [1].

The Strategic Defence Review will also emphasize an "always on" approach to munitions supply, aiming to keep Britain constantly prepared for war. The review is expected to warn about the changing nature of warfare, influenced by the use of drones and artificial intelligence, and propose measures such as teaching military values in schools and creating a new Home Guard to protect key infrastructure [1].

The increased spending on defence aligns with the government's plan to boost defence spending to 2.5% of national wealth by 2027 and potentially to 3% of GDP by 2034, should Labour win the next election [1]. This significant uplift in defence spending is expected to create skilled jobs and support economic growth [1].

Meanwhile, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte has proposed a 5% GDP defence spending target for alliance members at the upcoming Hague summit. This target aims to balance the Trump administration's demands while providing European allies with achievable goals. The proposal includes a two-tier spending model, with 3.5% of GDP allocated to core defence and equipment, and an additional 1.5% for broader investments in military mobility, infrastructure, and logistics [2].

These developments highlight the UK's and NATO's commitment to strengthening their military capabilities and ensuring collective security in an evolving geopolitical landscape.

item.title: Ford recalls more than 29,000 vehicles in the US, NHTSA says. - Reuters
item.description:
Ford recalls more than 29,000 vehicles in the US, NHTSA says. - Reuters

Ford Motor Company has issued a recall for over 29,000 vehicles in the United States due to a software error affecting the rearview camera system. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) announced the recall, which includes vehicles from the 2021 to 2024 model years. The issue, identified by the recall number 25V315000, can cause the rearview camera image to delay, freeze, or not display when the vehicle is in reverse [1].

The recall affects a variety of Ford models, including the F-150, Edge, Transit, Bronco, F-250, F-350, F-450, F-550, F-600, Lincoln Nautilus, Expedition, Escape, Mach-E, Mustang, Ranger, Navigator, and Corsair. Ford has stated that it is not aware of any injuries related to the recall, but it is aware of one allegation of a minor crash resulting in property damage [1].

Ford will address the issue by updating the vehicle software for free through dealers or through an over-the-air update. Owners can contact Ford customer service at 1-866-436-7332 and mention recall number 25S49. Alternatively, drivers can contact the NHTSA hotline at 888-327-4236, 888-275-9171, or at www.nhtsa.gov [1].

The recall comes after the NHTSA contacted Ford on January 17, 2025, about rearview camera complaints on 2021 to 2023 Ford F-150 vehicles. The NHTSA had 37 vehicle owner questionnaires, which Ford’s Automotive Safety Office reviewed. Ford found that in 15 of the questionnaires, drivers said their rearview camera images froze while in reverse [1].

The recall highlights the importance of regular software updates and maintenance for vehicle safety. It also underscores the need for consumers to stay informed about recalls and take necessary actions to ensure their vehicles are safe to operate.

item.description:
Opec+ to boost oil output for third consecutive month. - Financial Times

OPEC+ has announced plans to increase oil production for the third consecutive month, with expectations of a potential output hike in July. The decision was made during a meeting held on Saturday, with eight OPEC+ countries accelerating their output increases, led by Saudi Arabia and Russia. This move is aimed at regaining market share and addressing over-production by allies, despite Kazakhstan's refusal to cut production [2].

The meeting, conducted online at 0900 GMT, considered a larger output increase than the scheduled 411,000 barrels per day (bpd) for July. Analysts, such as Helima Croft of RBC Capital Markets, anticipate a 411,000 bpd rise, but the potential for a larger increase cannot be ruled out [2].

OPEC+ is aiming to unwind 2.2 million bpd of voluntary output cuts by key members, a move that has been driven by the need to address market volatility and external economic pressures. Oil prices, which had dropped to a four-year low in April, have shown some recovery, closing just below $63 per barrel on Friday [2].

The decision to boost oil output comes amidst heightened uncertainty over U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade tariffs. Oil prices fell in Asian trade on Friday and were headed for a weekly loss, with uncertainty over the economic impact of Trump’s tariffs weighing on the outlook for demand [1]. The legal sparring over Trump’s tariffs has sparked renewed concerns over their economic impact, leading to losses across most risk-driven assets.

The upcoming OPEC+ decision on output is expected to have a significant impact on global oil markets. Investors and financial professionals should closely monitor the developments, as the market remains volatile and sensitive to geopolitical and economic factors [2].

item.description:
Trump says he plans to double steel, aluminum tariffs to 50%. - Reuters

United States President Donald Trump has announced a significant increase in tariffs on steel and aluminum imports, raising the rates from 25 percent to 50 percent. This announcement was made during a rally in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, where Trump framed the tariff hike as a boost for the domestic manufacturing industry [1].

Trump's latest tariff increase comes amidst ongoing legal challenges and trade negotiations. The tariffs, initially imposed in 2018, have been the subject of multiple lawsuits and court rulings. In a recent development, a federal appeals court temporarily paused a ruling against Trump's global tariffs, allowing them to remain in effect while the administration pursues a formal appeal [2].

The tariff hike has been met with mixed reactions. Germany hopes for EU deal on sending failed asylum seekers to third countries, minister says - Reuters

Germany's interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, has expressed hope for a European Union-wide agreement on sending failed asylum seekers to third countries, according to Reuters [1]. This move is part of the country's effort to control immigration levels, which have been a significant political issue in recent years.

The proposal comes amid a national election victory for Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservatives, who campaigned on reducing immigration. Despite a decline in numbers over the past year, the issue remains contentious, with opinion polls indicating that many voters see immigration as being out of control.

Dobrindt emphasized the need for a Europe-wide consensus on the approach of using third countries to accommodate migrants who cannot return to their home countries. He stated that individual EU member states cannot implement this model independently and that it must be an EU-wide effort.

Earlier this month, the EU's executive commission proposed a scheme that would allow member states to reject asylum applications from migrants who passed through a "safe" third country on their way to the bloc. However, this proposal has faced criticism from rights groups and has yet to be adopted by national governments or the European Parliament.

Germany's plan to introduce more systematic land border checks for six months on people arriving by bus, train, or car from Schengen zone neighbors has sparked controversy. This move, which was announced by Interior Minister Nancy Faeser, aims to enhance border protection and deal with security threats. The plan has drawn criticism from neighboring countries, including Poland and Austria, which have expressed concerns about the potential economic impact and the treatment of rejected asylum seekers.

The German government's intention is to turn more people away and reduce irregular migration. However, experts warn that this could lead to a backlog of people stranded at borders and potentially set off a chain reaction among other EU member states. The move is seen as a response to security-related anxieties among voters rather than an effective answer to the security threats cited by the government.

Germany's stance on immigration has shifted significantly since the 2015 European migrant crisis, when the country largely opened its borders to refugees. The current policy reflects a broader trend in Europe, where countries are becoming more stringent with immigration controls.

item.description:
China's factory activity contracts in May, but there are signs of improvement - Bloomberg

China's factory activity contracted in May, according to the latest data from the National Bureau of Statistics. The official manufacturing purchasing managers' index (PMI) stood at 49.5, a slight improvement from April's 49.0, but still below the 50-point threshold that separates contraction from growth [1][2].

The non-manufacturing measure of activity in construction and services fell to 50.3 from 50.4 in April, while the composite index rose to 50.4. These PMI figures provide the first official snapshot of the health of the Chinese economy following a trade truce between Beijing and Washington [1].

The reprieve in tariffs has led to a surge in trade between China and the United States. Analysts have upgraded their forecasts for growth and exports this year, but deflationary pressures are expected to worsen, with China's economy-wide prices falling for two consecutive years [1].

Despite the improvement in factory activity, the outlook for manufacturing remains uncertain. The trade truce is only temporary, and tensions have risen again with the United States. The U.S. lowered tariffs to around 40%, but this level is still expected to reduce American imports from China by around 70% over the medium term [1].

Gross domestic product (GDP) is forecast to expand by 4.5% in 2025, significantly lower than the Chinese government's target of around 5%. Exports are expected to grow by 1.1% in 2025, an upgrade from the previous forecast of a 1% contraction [1].

The trade war has led to a two-front conflict for China, with the United States and the European Union imposing tariffs and export controls. China has restricted rare earth magnet exports, impacting industries globally, while the U.S. has banned semiconductor sales to Huawei and restricted exports for China's C919 aircraft [3].

The Geneva agreement to de-escalate the trade conflict has been cheered by investors, but the use of export controls as a weapon by both countries continues to threaten trade and global supply chains. The agreement has been seen as a major first step towards securing a final, comprehensive trade deal with China [3].

The approval follows a period of intense scrutiny and debate over the necessity and effectiveness of COVID-19 vaccines for various age groups and risk profiles. The CDC's new recommendations align with the World Health Organization's (WHO) guidelines, which do not recommend annual shots for healthy individuals under age 50, unless they have not been previously vaccinated against COVID-19. However, the WHO does recommend that pregnant women receive an updated COVID-19 vaccine during each pregnancy [2].

This development is part of a broader trend in public health policy, reflecting a shift towards more targeted and evidence-based approaches to vaccine recommendations. As the pandemic continues to evolve, these decisions will play a crucial role in shaping the future of COVID-19 vaccination strategies.

The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) has issued an emergency order directing Consumers Energy to delay the shutdown of its 1,560-MW coal-fired J.H. Campbell power plant in Michigan. The emergency order, citing potential power outages in the Midcontinent region this summer, extends the plant's operation beyond its planned May 31 shutdown. The DOE's decision was based on a report from the North American Electric Reliability Corp. (NERC), which found elevated risks of power outages during high demand or lower power output periods [1].

This is the 16th time the DOE has invoked its emergency authorities since August 2020, according to the agency. The order comes as the utility is planning to transition to cleaner energy sources, with the Campbell plant producing 6.6 million MWh in 2023, down from 7.7 million MWh in 2022 [1].

The DOE's action has sparked criticism from Public Citizen, which plans to challenge the order when Consumers Energy seeks cost recovery at the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission. The utility has stated it will comply with the order while working to determine appropriate cost recovery [1].

The emergency order follows a federal appeals court's temporary pause on a ruling against President Donald Trump's global tariffs, adding uncertainty to the tariffs' future [2].

Hormel Foods' (NYSE: HRL) shares have underperformed over the past year, losing 10%. The company has struggled with rising input costs and passing them on to customers without weakening volumes. Additionally, its Planters brand has faced challenges. In the company’s fiscal second quarter, Hormel earned $0.35, which beat estimates by a penny, as revenue was flat year over year at $2.9 billion. EPS was down about 8% from last year. Organic sales growth was 1%, though volumes were down 7%. Hormel has been able to raise prices to increase revenue and recapture some cost, but clearly, consumers remain very price sensitive, leading to a nearly equally sized drop-off in volumes. This reflects a difficult operating environment with limited discretionary income. On the earnings call, management said the retail environment is “choppy” with a strained consumer, which, I believe, is a fair description of the environment. Lower volumes reduced operating efficiencies, and as such, Hormel reported just a 16.7% gross margin. Even though sales rose by $11 million, gross profit fell by $19 million, reflecting some of these pressures. The company is closing a plant in California, moving that production to its two remaining plants, which should help improve unit costs. Given lower gross profit, operating income fell by $17 million to $248 million as margins compressed 50bps to 8.6%. These pressures came even as there are some tangible benefits to management’s cost-cutting effort, the transformation and modernize (T&M) initiative. Management reiterated $100-$150 million of benefits from this program this year. Validating this claim, SG&A was $15 million lower at $251 million. One headwind for activity in the quarter was that HRL pulled back on advertising ahead of a large push in H2. Advertising spending was $36 million, down $8 million from last year. It expects advertising costs to rise double-digits in H2, largely to support new products from Planters, SPAM, and other key brands [1].

Looking at segment results, retail accounts for 60% of the business. Here, sales were flat despite a 7% drop in volume, thanks to price increases. Thanks to cost cuts from its T&M program, profits rose by 4%. Lower commodity shipments drove the sales decline. Importantly, Planters is showing sequential improvement (though still declining), and its Applegate brand reaccelerated to 6% sales growth. Its Mexican offerings are also growing, thanks to strength from Herdez. Hormel Planters has been posting declines, but management expects sales growth to turn positive later this year, given its new marketing push. New product launches, including its nut “duo” packs, have helped to liven the brand, and an ongoing focus on protein-oriented and healthy snacking should be a favorable trend for the brand. Applegate has seen strong take-up of its breakfast offerings. Foodservice volume was down 1%, excluding the impact of divestitures. Due to price increases, organic net sales rose by 4% to $936 million. Profits fell by 4%, given margin pressure, and it is seeing end-market softness. This unit is particularly exposed to traffic at convenience stores, and consumer spending on snacks here can be quite discretionary. Given the tepid consumer environment, I struggle to see a case for much acceleration here [1].

Hormel finally, international volume rose 9%, but profits fell by 21%. It has seen solid exports and strong growth in China, in particular, where it operates locally. Brazil was a source of weakness. This unit is just about 7% of the business, and so the ultimate impact is negligible. The US is a net exporter of agriculture products, so insofar as trade tensions lead to countervailing duties, that could pose a risk. Importantly, it has a local presence within China, which insulates it from some of these trade pressures. Hormel One key segment for the business is Turkey, where supply has been a source of pressure, which has weakened margins. It has taken time to pass increases on to consumers, though its shift towards value-add products has helped to insulate it somewhat. Management is seeing some sequential improvement in pricing and believes most costs will be recaptured during the key “whole bird” Thanksgiving selling season [1].

Hormel has a strong balance sheet, with $670 million of cash and $2.9 billion of debt. Especially as pre-summer inventory builds reverse, we should see strong free cash flow generation over the balance of the year, and with debt already at the low end of target, Hormel has capacity for bolt-on M&A or further dividend growth. Shares have a 3.9% dividend yield. Management is committed to dividend growth, with 59 years of increase. I expect that streak to continue. With $1.62 of forward earnings power, I see Hormel trading with an ~18.7x multiple. This is not a compelling entry point, especially for a stock that is flat over the past decade and down over a third in the past five years. Hormel’s guidance is aggressive, and I see downside risk, given rising input costs and questions about how quickly it can reaccelerate Planters' sales. Given its balance sheet and the likelihood of some improvement, I do not see a rush to sell shares, and ~$30 strikes me as fair value for a low-growth company with a solid balance sheet and secure dividend [1].
